planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, allowing room for a large, vigorous canopy with long, zigzagging shoots.

directions: Mu is one of the oldest Chinese jujube selections grown in the United States, brought over by USDA plant explorer Frank Meyer in the early twentieth century and still maintained in germplasm collections today. The tree grows notably large and vigorous compared to many modern jujube cultivars, sending out long shoots with curving side branches that benefit from occasional thinning to keep the canopy open and fruit within reach. Fruit size on Mu tends to run medium but is less uniform from year to year than on more refined modern cultivars, so it is grown today mainly by collectors and jujube enthusiasts interested in preserving historic germplasm rather than for commercial fresh-market production. Like other jujubes, Mu tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, making it a low-input option for a Gulf Coast fruit collection.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension (Guide H-340)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Shuimen grows into a moderately upright small tree well suited to a mixed fruit orchard row.

directions: Shuimen is a historic Chinese jujube cultivar originally collected in Shanxi Province and introduced to the United States by USDA plant explorer Frank Meyer in the early twentieth century, and it remains part of the living germplasm collections used to study jujube diversity today. The fruit is midsize and elongated, tapering toward the blossom end, and it ripens early to midseason, ahead of later cultivars like Lang. Shuimen fruit is dual-purpose, eaten fresh off the tree or dried, and the tree itself has a moderately upright habit with medium to high yields once established. As with other jujubes, little irrigation and no regular spray program are needed once the tree is past its first few establishment years.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension (Guide H-340)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, training a central leader early since Yu naturally grows tall with relatively few side branches.

directions: Yu is another of the historic Chinese jujube selections introduced to the United States by USDA plant explorer Frank Meyer in the early twentieth century and preserved in jujube germplasm collections ever since. The fruit is large and elongated, tapering toward the stylar end, with reddish-brown skin covering sweet, firm flesh typical of good fresh-eating jujubes. The tree grows distinctly tall with large leaves and fewer side branches than many other jujube cultivars, giving it a more open, upright silhouette that benefits from early structural pruning. Yu is of interest mainly to jujube collectors and breeding programs working with historic germplasm rather than being a widely sold nursery item.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension (Guide H-340)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Jixin grows upright and produces a reliable medium yield of fruit best harvested for drying.

directions: Jixin, whose Chinese name translates roughly to 'chicken heart' for its tapered shape, originates from Henan Province and was imported into the United States by New Mexico State University in 2011 as part of ongoing jujube cultivar trials in the Southwest. The fruit is midsize and elongated to cylindrical with a slight taper at the blossom end, and it is notable for unusually high sugar content, which along with its shiny skin makes it an excellent choice for drying into a date-like dried fruit. The tree has an upright growth habit and produces a medium, fairly consistent yield once established. Because it was selected and trialed specifically for hot, arid growing conditions, Jixin is a reasonable candidate for Gulf Coast heat, though it has less of a track record in humid climates than older, more widely distributed cultivars like Li and Lang.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension (Guide H-340)
New Mexico State University Sustainable Agriculture Science Center
